questions.prompt: Which of these is dynamic testing?
options: Reviewing a user story with the product owner
Running a linter on source code
Executing a test case against the deployed login page
Inspecting a database design document
questions.explanation: Dynamic testing executes the software. Reviews, linters and design inspections examine work products without executing them, so they are static.

questions.prompt: Test cases themselves can be reviewed statically.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Almost any readable work product can be statically tested, including test cases, test plans and requirements.

questions.prompt: Which ISTQB review type is the least formal?
options: Inspection
Technical review
Walkthrough
Informal review
questions.explanation: Informal reviews have no defined process or documented output. Walkthroughs, technical reviews and inspections are progressively more formal, with inspection the most formal.

questions.prompt: A static analysis tool reviews this code without running it. Which finding is it able to report?
options: The function returns the wrong total for a real customer
`discount` may be referenced before assignment when `is_member` is False
The page loads slowly
A user cannot find the checkout button
questions.explanation: Data-flow analysis can see that `discount` is only assigned inside the if branch. The other findings need execution or real users.

questions.prompt: Which defects are typically easier to find with static testing than with dynamic testing? Select all that apply.
options: Ambiguous or contradictory requirements
Unreachable code and unused variables
Memory leaks visible only under 8 hours of load
Deviations from coding standards
questions.explanation: Ambiguities, unreachable code and standard violations are visible in the work product itself. Load-related memory leaks only appear when the system runs, so dynamic testing is needed.

questions.prompt: What is the output difference between static and dynamic testing?
options: Static testing finds failures; dynamic finds defects
Static testing finds defects directly; dynamic testing observes failures, which then have to be traced back to defects
Both find only failures
Static testing finds nothing until code is executed
questions.explanation: Because static testing reads the work product, it points to the defect itself. Dynamic testing sees behaviour (failures) and debugging locates the defect.

questions.prompt: A team runs inspections but finds nothing useful: reviewers open the document for the first time in the meeting. Which part of the review process is missing?
options: Planning
Individual review (preparation) before the review meeting
Fixing and reporting
Choosing a tool
questions.explanation: Individual review is where most issues are found. Without it, meeting time is spent reading rather than discussing anomalies.

questions.prompt: A user story says: 'As a user I want to reset my password so I can log in again.' In a 10-minute review, which question finds the most serious gap before coding?
options: Which font should the reset page use?
How long is the reset link valid, can it be reused, and what happens to existing sessions after reset?
Should the button be blue?
Can we add a dark mode?
questions.explanation: Token lifetime, single use and session invalidation are security-critical behaviours missing from the story. Static review finds them before any code is built; cosmetic questions are lower value.

questions.prompt: A manager proposes: 'We now have a static analysis tool on every commit, so we can drop most system tests.' What is the best answer?
options: Agree: static analysis finds all defects
Disagree: static analysis finds code-level issues but cannot reveal wrong behaviour against requirements, integration, performance or usability failures; both approaches complement each other
Agree only for back-end code
Disagree because static tools are always wrong
questions.explanation: Static and dynamic testing find different kinds of problems. Static tools are valuable but cannot tell you the system meets its requirements when it actually runs.
